name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 23 December 1967

clue.text: Just the girl for the opera

definitions.text: Just the girl for the opera

blocks.note: surface reading: a young woman ideally suited to a night at the opera house
setter's reading: the title of an opera by Balfe names its heroine by her homeland, a gypsy girl from central Europe

explanation.walkthrough: The Bohemian Girl (1843) is a popular English opera by Michael Balfe, and Puccini's La Boheme is also full of such girls.
explanation.definitionFit: A Bohemian is a native of Bohemia, the gypsy heroine in the title of Balfe's well-known opera.

clue.text: Curtsied — for apples?

definitions.note: a verb phrase: ducked for apples

blocks.note: first meaning: made a quick bob, a small dip of the knees
second meaning: ducked the head into water to catch floating apples, a party game

explanation.walkthrough: Bobbing for apples is a Halloween party game: players try to grab apples floating in a tub using only their teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: A bob is both a brief bending of the knees in respect and the dipping motion of the apple game.

clue.text: Yearn to be a wool holder?

blocks.note: first meaning: long for something, crave
second meaning, a playful invention: one who holds a hank, a coiled skein of yarn

explanation.surface: Someone wishes they could spend life minding the wool.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second reading as a made-up word: HANK plus the -ER of a doer.
explanation.definitionFit: To hanker after something is to long for it persistently, a close synonym of the verb.

clue.text: "How many loved your — of glad grace" (Yeats)

definitions.text: "How many loved your — of glad grace" (Yeats)

blocks.clueFragment: "How many loved your — of glad grace"
blocks.note: a line from Yeats's poem When You Are Old with a word missing
the missing word is the brief spells of time in which the beloved's grace was glad

explanation.walkthrough: The full line reads 'How many loved your moments of glad grace, / And loved your beauty with love false or true'.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural noun means brief instants of time, the passing spells of happy grace Yeats recalls.

clue.text: What match hath Anne?

blocks.note: surface reading: which husband or which game does Anne have?
setter's reading: Shakespeare's wife Anne, whose surname begins with 'hath' and ends with a kind of fixture played on the opponent's ground

explanation.walkthrough: Anne Hathaway was Shakespeare's wife; split her surname as HATH plus the rest and you have the kind of match played at the other team's ground.
explanation.definitionFit: An away match is a game played at the opposing side's ground, not one's own home venue.

clue.text: Dismount to succeed in a flirtation

blocks.note: first meaning: climb down from a horse or bicycle
second meaning: the British slang '... with someone', to pair up romantically

explanation.surface: A rider climbs down from the saddle to win over an admirer.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang, to get off with someone is to start a romantic or sexual encounter with them.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both alighting from a mount and, colloquially, pairing up with a romantic partner.

clue.text: What's in a letter? Sleep it off

definitions.note: a noun phrase: the written text that a letter contains

indicators.note: something gone off is spoilt or out of order, so the preceding words are jumbled

blocks.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks what a letter says and is told to go and sleep off a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sleep it off' reads as advice to someone drunk, but 'off' is the signal to rework the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: An epistle is a formal letter, especially the New Testament letters of the apostles read aloud in church.

clue.text: Bringing good news from Ghent to Aix, they did

definitions.text: Bringing good news from Ghent to Aix, they did

blocks.clueFragment: Bringing good news from Ghent to Aix
blocks.note: surface reading: Browning's poem How They Brought the Good News from Ghent to Aix, about a desperate gallop
setter's reading: the riders drove their horses too hard, two of the three horses dying of exhaustion

explanation.walkthrough: In Browning's poem three riders gallop through the night; two horses collapse on the way and only Roland reaches Aix.
explanation.definitionFit: To override a horse is to ride it to exhaustion, which literally describes the riders in Browning's ride.

clue.text: What have ton-up boys and devout abstainers in common?

definitions.text: What have ton-up boys and devout abstainers in common?

blocks.note: surface reading: 1960s British motorcyclists who raced at a ton, a hundred miles an hour, enjoying their speedy outings
setter's reading: religious people who go without food on appointed holy days

explanation.walkthrough: Ton-up boys were young British bikers of the 1950s and 60s who aimed to hit 100 mph; their days out are speedy ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Fast days are days of religious abstinence from food, and punningly days spent travelling at high speed.

clue.text: What Mother Hubbard sought might have been found in the garden shed!

definitions.text: What Mother Hubbard sought might have been found in the garden shed!

blocks.note: surface reading: the nursery rhyme in which Old Mother Hubbard goes to the cupboard to fetch her dog a bone

blocks.clueFragment: might have been found in the garden shed!
blocks.note: setter's reading: gardeners keep a sack of ground-up animal skeleton fertiliser in the shed

explanation.walkthrough: Old Mother Hubbard found the cupboard bare; the joke is that the dog's dinner was sitting as fertiliser in the shed.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonemeal is crushed animal skeleton used as a garden fertiliser, and punningly a dinner of bone.

clue.text: Wildfowl in variety

definitions.note: an adjective sense: various, of several kinds

blocks.note: first meaning: water birds such as loons that plunge underwater for fish
second meaning: the archaic adjective meaning sundry or several

explanation.surface: A naturalist notes many kinds of wild birds on the lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divers' as an adjective is an old word for several or assorted, as in 'divers reasons'.
explanation.definitionFit: Divers are loons, swimming birds that hunt underwater, and the old adjective means assorted or sundry.

clue.text: Archdeacon at Brighton edifice in ducal territory

blocks.note: an archdeacon is styled the Venerable, abbreviated Ven
the Brighton Dome is a concert hall beside the Royal Pavilion

explanation.surface: A senior clergyman visits a seaside building somewhere in a duke's lands.
explanation.walkthrough: An archdeacon's title is 'the Venerable'; the Dome is a well-known entertainment venue in Brighton, a resort on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Vendome was a French duchy on the Loir, held by the Bourbon dukes of that name.

clue.text: They go out by direction

blocks.note: surface reading: people leaving because they have been told to
setter's reading: a stage direction in a play script, the Latin word for several actors leaving

explanation.walkthrough: 'Direction' means a stage direction, the printed instruction in a script telling actors when to move.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin stage instruction tells several actors to leave the stage together, the plural of exit.

clue.text: The nature of Love lace's ocular attachment?

definitions.text: The nature of Love lace's ocular attachment?

blocks.note: surface reading: some lace trim fixed around an eye, perhaps a decorative patch
setter's reading: the poet Richard Lovelace, whose To Althea, from Prison has him bound to his lady's eye

explanation.walkthrough: Lovelace's poem opens 'When Love with unconfined wings / Hovers within my gates', and he lies 'fettered to her eye'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fettered means chained or shackled, the poet's image of being bound captive by his beloved's gaze.

clue.text: Hurried round to court and then pounced

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: hurried means went fast
to court a sweetheart is to woo them

explanation.surface: Someone rushed off to court a lover, then leapt on them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like an adverb describing the hurry, but it tells you to wrap one word around the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A hawk that swoops dives down suddenly upon its prey, the same action as pouncing.

clue.text: The first of forty 8

blocks.note: surface reading: the opening item of a set of forty
setter's reading: the answer to 8 down, days of abstinence; forty of them make up Lent

explanation.walkthrough: The 8 points to 8 down, FAST DAYS; the forty days of Lent begin on this Wednesday.
explanation.definitionFit: The Christian season of Lent opens on this Wednesday, starting forty days of fasting before Easter.

clue.text: Furnish the elderly with tea-things for example?

blocks.note: to furnish someone with gear is to equip them
the elderly can be summed up as old age

explanation.surface: A charity supplies old people with a tea set.
explanation.walkthrough: An equipage was an old word for a set of articles for a purpose, such as a tea equipage of pot, cups and caddy.
explanation.definitionFit: Equipage once meant any complete outfit of utensils, so a full tea service is one example of it.

clue.text: Highlanders arrive by two waterways

definitions.note: the regiment named the Seaforth Highlanders

blocks.note: the first waterway: open sea
the second waterway: the River Forth in Scotland

explanation.surface: Scottish soldiers land by ship after sailing two stretches of water.
explanation.walkthrough: The Forth is the Scottish river flowing past Stirling into the Firth of Forth by Edinburgh.
explanation.definitionFit: The Seaforth Highlanders were a famous Scottish infantry regiment of the British Army until 1961.

clue.text: This calls for an answer

blocks.note: surface reading: a summons or challenge that demands a reply
setter's reading: the punctuation symbol placed after a query

explanation.walkthrough: The clue sounds like a challenge or a letter needing a reply; it is the punctuation sign that ends a query.
explanation.definitionFit: The symbol closing an interrogative sentence signals that a reply is expected from the reader.

clue.text: Whatever this artist does goes with a swing

definitions.text: Whatever this artist does goes with a swing

blocks.note: surface reading: a performer whose every act is a lively success
setter's reading: a circus acrobat performing on a bar hung from ropes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes with a swing' is an idiom for being a lively success; here it is literal, and the artist names the performer by their apparatus.
explanation.definitionFit: A trapeze is the swinging bar on which an aerial circus artist performs, here standing for the act.

clue.text: The trapdoor victim of Cumnor Place

definitions.text: The trapdoor victim of Cumnor Place

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who fell through a hidden hatch
setter's reading: the wife of Robert Dudley, who died in a fall at Cumnor Place in 1560

explanation.walkthrough: Amy Robsart, wife of Elizabeth I's favourite Robert Dudley, was found dead at the foot of stairs; Scott's novel Kenilworth has her fall through a trapdoor.
explanation.definitionFit: Amy Robsart died at Cumnor Place, Oxfordshire, and in Walter Scott's Kenilworth she plunges through a trapdoor.

clue.text: "Can Love be controlled by —'?" Polly inquired

definitions.text: "Can Love be controlled by —'?" Polly inquired

blocks.note: a line from a song in John Gay's The Beggar's Opera with a word missing
Polly Peachum sings it when her parents counsel her against marrying Macheath

explanation.walkthrough: In The Beggar's Opera (1728) Polly sings 'Can Love be controll'd by advice? / Will Cupid our mothers obey?'
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is counsel or guidance, which Polly's parents give her about her choice of husband.

clue.text: Conductors in court

blocks.note: surface reading: orchestra leaders or bus conductors
setter's reading: officials who show people to their seats and keep order in a courtroom

explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductors' suggests music or buses; here it is people who conduct, that is lead, others to their places.
explanation.definitionFit: Court officials who escort witnesses and the public and keep order are literally guides or conductors.

clue.text: Is there in Lippo Lippi a revolutionary light?

blocks.note: taken as written
the painter was Fra Lippo Lippi, Fra being the title of an Italian friar
a red is a communist revolutionary

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether the Renaissance painter-monk was secretly a radical.
explanation.walkthrough: Browning's poem is titled Fra Lippo Lippi; Fra means brother, the title of a friar.
explanation.definitionFit: Infrared is radiation beyond the red end of the visible spectrum, often loosely called a kind of light.

clue.text: A body's involved following Byron's bride

definitions.note: the word that follows 'The Bride of' in Byron's title

indicators.note: involved means tangled or convoluted, so the letters are knotted into a new order

blocks.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A corpse turns up in a case concerning Byron's new wife.
explanation.walkthrough: Byron wrote the poem The Bride of Abydos (1813); the town on the Hellespont completes the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Abydos is the ancient town on the Hellespont named in the title of Byron's Turkish tale.

clue.text: How the corncrake does go on

definitions.text: How the corncrake does go on

blocks.note: setter's reading: the corncrake is a bird of the crake family, a land species of that name
surface reading: the bird's harsh, endless call, like someone complaining at length

explanation.walkthrough: The corncrake is a kind of rail; to rail is also to complain bitterly and at length.
explanation.definitionFit: To rail is to rant or complain vehemently, and the corncrake belongs to the bird family of that name.

clue.text: Homes that take pride of place

definitions.text: Homes that take pride of place

blocks.clueFragment: Homes that take pride of place
blocks.note: surface reading: the finest houses in a street, the showpieces
setter's reading: lofty nests of eagles, proud birds that build on high crags

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pride of place' means the top position; eagles, emblems of pride, nest at the very highest points.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the nests of eagles or other birds of prey, built high on cliffs or treetops.

clue.text: Explosive publication?

definitions.note: stands for a store of explosives

blocks.note: first meaning: a store for gunpowder and ammunition
second meaning: a periodical with articles and pictures

explanation.walkthrough: Read together the words suggest a scandalous journal; apart, each is one sense of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an arsenal for gunpowder and a periodical issued weekly or monthly.

clue.text: "Our — roll from soul to soul" (Tennyson)

blocks.note: a line from the bugle song in Tennyson's The Princess with a word missing
the missing word is the repeated sounds that answer the bugle across the glens

explanation.walkthrough: The song ends 'Our echoes roll from soul to soul, / And grow for ever and for ever'.
explanation.definitionFit: Echoes are reflected sounds repeating back, which Tennyson contrasts with fading bugle notes in the hills.

clue.text: Bets stimulated in the columbaries by visitors from 26?

definitions.text: stimulated in the columbaries by visitors from 26?
definitions.note: a noun sense: the agitated flapping caused there

blocks.note: first meaning: British slang for small wagers

blocks.clueFragment: stimulated in the columbaries by visitors from 26?
blocks.note: second meaning: the panicky wing-beating among doves in a dovecote when eagles from their nests come calling

explanation.walkthrough: A columbarium is a dovecote; the visitors are eagles from 26 across. In Britain a flutter is a small bet.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun means both a modest gamble and a nervous flapping of wings or general agitation.
